2.0.0.en: 1 I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity. 2 I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it? 3 I thought in mine heart to cheer my body with wine, my heart meditating on wisdom, and to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was that good for the sons of men, which they should do under the heaven all the days of their life.

2.0.1.en: The Preacher (Qoheleth) tried to find what he sought in frenzied pleasure or sensual excitement, so he turned to bodily delights as a source that might give him satisfaction; he went on drawing from the sensual pleasures of food, which are symbolized by wine, and they gave him a passing, temporary pleasure, not lasting satisfaction.

2.0.3.en: Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure (enjoy happiness).

2.0.4.en: And, behold, this also is vanity.

2.0.5.en: I said of laughter, It is mad!

2.0.6.en: And of mirth, What doeth it?!" [1-2].

2.0.7.en: Solomon communed with his heart instead of discussing the matter with God in a spirit of prayer and godliness, saying: Try laughter, eating and drinking (wine), drive away care and enjoy happiness; just as the rich fool said, "And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Lk 12:19).

2.0.8.en: Many think that happiness lies in a life of amusement, parties and temporal joys, with the eating, drinking, entertainment and laughter they contain... These do not distinguish between inner joy, which gives constant cheerfulness and true peace, and the laughter of amusement, which springs from an inner emptiness. Inner joy is food for the soul; it nourishes it and makes it grow, so that it widens to carry within it the joyful Kingdom of God. But temporal joy outside the circle of God numbs man and does not satisfy his depths, but rather increases his sorrow... Therefore the wise man calls it mad! Many resort to drugs and bad companions to escape their problems, and behold, they throw themselves into graver problems that touch their inner being.

2.0.9.en: He said of laughter, "It is mad," because it cannot turn the heart to true happiness, but only offers a temporary covering for inner sorrow and hidden bitterness. And perhaps he calls it so because it urges him to go far from God, who is "the true joy," for it is said: "They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ. They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave. Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways" (Job 21:12-14).

2.0.10.en: He says to outward joy, What doeth it? For he realizes that laughter does not reform the heart and does not remove its gloom. Therefore it is said: "He that singeth songs to a heavy (troubled) heart" (Prov 25:20)... Instead of amusement it would have befitted him to resort to the tears of repentance, which give inner joy and sincere cheerfulness, because sin breaks the heart and fills it with bitter gloom!

2.1.0.en: Along with laughter or amusement, Solomon resorted to drinking wine, thinking that he was able to cheer his body with wine while his heart meditated on wisdom [3]; that is, he drank it in order to gain experience and to see whether wine could satisfy his life, but he found folly in it, because "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging, and whosoever reeleth thereby is not wise" (Prov 20:1). In this he is like one who wanted to serve God and mammon at the same time.

2.1.1.en: St. Basil the Great speaks to us about the danger of pursuing pleasures, saying: [Animals are earthly and incline toward the earth... their heads are bowed toward the ground, and they look to their bellies, searching for the things that please them. But you, O man, your head is lifted toward heaven, and your eyes look upward; so if you are defiled with the lusts of the flesh, and are enslaved to the pleasures of the belly and the lower pleasures, you thereby draw near to the unreasoning animals and become like them. I propose to you to care for another matter that befits you: "Seek those things which are above, where Christ is" (Col 3:1). Rise above the passing things of the world, and learn from your bodily constitution, and make it a rule for your life. Your city is heaven, and your true homeland is the Jerusalem above, and your fellow citizens are the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven].

2.1.2.en: Again he says: [Philosophers and thinkers were eager to search for the end of man on this earth. But they differed among themselves in this matter, their opinions conflicted and their schools multiplied. Some of them claimed that the end of man is knowledge, while others said it is work. Some said that the end of man is to despise the body and subject it to the control of the mind, and to strengthen the spirit and regard it as the greatest power in man, while others said that the end of man in this life is only the enjoyment of pleasures and the good things of life. As for us, the end we seek and aspire to reach with all care and diligence is the blessed life with God in the everlasting heaven, and nothing in the world equals this praiseworthy pursuit in honor and greatness for the rational creature].

2.2.0.en: 4 I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards: 5 I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits: 6 I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees: 7 I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me: 8 I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, a lady and ladies. 9 So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me. 10 And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour. 11 Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.

2.2.1.en: The Preacher furnished himself with worldly delights, magnificent buildings, slaves, silver and gold, and the things that belong to kings alone; yet this was not from a regression to, or an escape into, uncommitted childhood, as the Greeks did, immersed in pleasures and occupied with appearances to escape responsibility. As it is written in the Book of Wisdom: "For they said within themselves, reasoning not aright, Our life is short and sorrowful... Come on therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present, and use pleasures in the wilderness while it is the time of old age, and let us fill ourselves with excellent wine and perfumes, and let no breeze of the flowers of spring pass us by..." (Wis 2:1, 6, 7).

2.2.2.en: Rather, it was the custom of the Jews to express power by holding feasts and building magnificent buildings, and in short, by becoming a master of the arts.

2.2.3.en: a. He was deeply absorbed in construction and building, in cities as in villages, for he says: "I builded me houses" [4]. It was said of him: "And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the LORD, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer... And all the cities of store that Solomon had, and cities for his chariots, and cities for his horsemen, and that which Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion" (1 Kgs 9:15-19). He built many buildings, but he began by building the house of the Lord, not like those to whom it was said: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" (Hag 1:3)... He also employed many poor workers for their benefit. This is the good side of Solomon in his concern for construction and building; but perhaps what spoiled his work for a time was his thinking that these projects could satisfy his soul and quench his desire for temporal glory, for he says: "I made me great works" [4].

2.2.4.en: Building houses is not a sin, but the sin is to be occupied with building houses for the comfort of our bodies without offering a house to the Lord in our depths. Let the Lord rest in our hearts, and He will give rest to our bodies also, and will kindle our hearts with the fire of love, so that we long to depart and dwell with Him and rest in His divine embrace, instead of being occupied with temporal greatness and vain glory. Let the Lord dwell in our hearts as His own house, and let us dwell in His heavens as our own eternal home, and the whole world will not be able to draw us to itself.

2.2.5.en: * He who flees from vain glory with understanding tastes in himself (the hope of) the age to come.

2.2.6.en: * As soon as a man chooses to be free from possessions, his mind is occupied with departing from the world; he makes the life after the resurrection his constant meditation, and strives toward constant readiness (for departure), which is profitable to him; he begins to despise everything that brings (temporal) honor or bodily comfort, and this penetrates his thoughts, and his mind is always refreshed by thinking of despising the world.

2.2.7.en: St. Isaac the Syrian The Fathers urge us to build the inner house of the Lord, His temple and His altar, in our hearts:

2.2.8.en: * Make me worthy, my Lord Jesus Christ, to take part in building Your house...!

2.2.9.en: But the dwelling of the Lord that He wants us to build is holiness... By this every man can set up a tabernacle for God within his heart.

2.2.10.en: * Let the soul have an altar in the midst of the heart, on which the sacrifices of prayer and the burnt offerings of mercy are offered, and upon it the bulls of pride are slaughtered with the knife of meekness, and the rams of anger and the goats of luxury and lusts are killed...

2.2.11.en: Let the soul know how to set up, within the holy of holies of its heart, a lampstand that shines without ceasing!

2.2.12.en: Origen b. He cared for planting gardens: "I planted vineyards for myself; I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits" [4-5].

2.2.13.en: God gave the first man the garden of Eden to work in, containing trees of every fruit, and also including the tree of life... So God wants to satisfy the body with every temporal fruit and to satisfy the soul with the tree of immortal life, but man cared for what satisfies his body and not his soul. Therefore the Lord Christ came to our earth, and His body was hung on the tree, that we may stretch out our hands and pluck from it the fruit of life. Let the Cross be planted in our souls and let us gather the fruit of the Holy Spirit in us, so that our view of every fruit may be sanctified, and man may be satisfied in body and spirit.

2.2.14.en: Our Christ plants His Cross in our hearts and sets up from it a joyful paradise, bearing the fruit of the Holy Spirit that gladdens heavenly and earthly beings!

2.3.0.en: c. He made many channels for watering: "I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees" [6].

2.3.1.en: We need the fountain of living water, that is, the Holy Spirit of God, who waters our inner wilderness and sets up from it a holy garden.

2.4.0.en: d. He got servants and maidens who bore him servants born in the house for his service [7].

2.4.1.en: e. He got cattle, silver, gold and the peculiar treasure of kings [7-8]. He became extremely rich, for it was said of him: "And the king made silver to be in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars made he to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale, for abundance" (1 Kgs 10:27).

2.4.2.en: What does "the peculiar treasure of kings" mean? What belongs to kings, or what kings alone, among all the nobles and great men, have of possessions or particular property.

2.4.3.en: The expression "peculiar treasure" in Hebrew, s’qulia, basically means "property," but it came to be used generally for property of high value. The people of God were called "a people of possession" (Ex 19:5), as a people whom God chose to be His portion, and who are exceedingly precious in His eyes.

2.4.4.en: Solomon acquired what belongs to kings as a precious thing... But to you the King of kings Himself is offered, that you may possess Him and He may possess you; you become His portion and He is your portion, and you say, "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine." This is what satisfies your inner depths, which God created in His image, and no one else can satisfy them!

2.4.5.en: The Preacher has shown in more than one place that wealth and possessions are not an evil thing; rather, the evil lies in the corruption of our will and our wrong view of them, and also in the deviation of our aim:

2.4.6.en: * Be watchful in using your riches, lest God's gift to you remain useless in your hands.

2.4.7.en: Do you have gold and silver? If you handle them well, they will be good for you. And if you are wicked, you will misuse them.

2.4.8.en: Gold and silver are evil to the wicked and good to the righteous, not because gold and silver make men righteous, but because righteous men use them for good...

2.4.9.en: What use is what you have in your possession, when you do not possess the One who gave you everything?!...

2.4.10.en: Do you want to keep your wealth? Manage it as you wish; if you find a better guardian for it than Christ, hand it over to him...

2.4.11.en: Christ is with you to take your money and keep it for you; He will not betray you, but will carry your treasure faithfully.

2.4.12.en: St. Augustine In the second century St. Clement of Alexandria wrote a book entitled "Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?" in which he explains the Christian view of wealth; in it he says:

2.4.13.en: [We do not cast the rich man to the ground, he who benefits our brethren...

2.4.14.en: Man does not squander his wealth; rather it befits him to destroy his inner lusts that conflict with the good use of wealth. For when a man becomes virtuous and good, he can use this wealth in a good way.

2.4.15.en: So let us understand the leaving of our possessions (Mk 10:17-31) and the selling of them as a leaving and selling of the lusts of our souls].

2.5.0.en: f. He provided for himself, to no avail, every licentious atmosphere of male singers and female singers, a lady and ladies [8]... He did not deprive his body or his heart of material or immaterial pleasures.

2.6.0.en: With the riches and pleasures he enjoyed, he gained temporal glory and his human wisdom remained with him, for he says: "So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me" [9].

2.7.0.en: But the experience he gained from all this is: "Whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy... Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun" [10-11].

2.7.1.en: God wants our rest and our joy, but our preoccupation with the pleasures and wealth of the world often draws our heart away from the rest that is in Christ Jesus, and from the enjoyment of fellowship in the heavenly glories.

2.7.2.en: * The mind of the man who flees from the comfort of this age gazes intently at the age to come. He who is captive to possessions is their slave.

2.7.3.en: * Blessed is the man who stops his ears to all the delights that separate him from his Creator, for he eats only one delicious food from the table of the Most High, the food on which the heavenly powers feed.

2.7.4.en: Blessed is he who takes as his food the living Bread that came down from heaven, that Bread that gives light to the world, that supports the ages of the new world.

2.7.5.en: Blessed is he who sees in his drink the watered spring of life, flowing from the bosom of the Father in His mercy; for when he drinks from it his eyes are fixed on Him, his heart rejoices and flourishes anew, and is filled with joy and gladness. He who beholds his Lord in his food is content with Him and enjoys fellowship with Him alone, and has no fellowship with the unworthy lest he be deprived of His splendor...

2.7.6.en: The man who has friends for the purpose of filling his belly is like a wolf feeding on carrion!

2.7.7.en: How terrible is your greed, you fool, for you want to fill your belly with every lust!

2.7.8.en: These warnings are sufficient for those who are able to control their bellies.

2.7.9.en: * He who is occupied with many concerns is a slave to many, but he who abandons them all and cares only for himself is a friend of God!

2.7.10.en: * Lord, count me worthy to hate my (temporal) life for the sake of the life that is in You!

2.7.11.en: St. Isaac the Syrian The Fathers of the Church give us their spiritual experience regarding the enjoyment of bodily pleasures, summed up in the necessity of keeping to the middle or moderate way, which they call the royal way.

2.7.12.en: * Do not fill your belly too much, lest fornication torment you, and do not weaken your body, lest those who hate you rejoice over you.

2.7.13.en: Hold to a moderate rank, and behold, you are walking the royal way, and your journey will be without fear.

2.8.0.en: St. John Saba The Preacher sums up his experience with worldly pleasures, saying: "Behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun" [11].

2.8.1.en: * The Preacher says, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." But if all creation is good as the work of the hands of the good Creator, how can everything be vain? If the earth is vain, are the heavens also vain...? And also the angels, thrones, dominions, powers and the rest of the orders? Never! If things that are good in themselves, as the creation of the good Creator, have been called vain, it is only by comparison with what is higher and greater than they. For example, if a lamp is compared with a lantern, it is counted less than it; and if the lantern is compared with a star, it gives no light at all. And if a star shines, it grows pale before the moon, and the moon appears dim before the sun, and if the sun is compared with Christ, it is counted darkness. So God says, "I AM THAT I AM"; when all creatures are compared with Him, they are counted as non-existent.

2.8.2.en: St. Jerome The author concludes his discourse on sensual pleasures by saying: "And there was no profit under the sun" [11]. It is as though he were saying: Who will carry me to what is above the sun? Who will lift me above time? I need the Lord Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, and the wisdom of God.

2.8.3.en: Thus he moves from the unsatisfying sensual pleasures to speak of temporal wisdom, which, though better than ignorance or folly, cannot satisfy the soul as the wisdom of God does!

2.9.s.en: 3. The vanity of pursuing human wisdom:

2.9.0.en: 12 And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly: for what is the man who cometh after the king, whom they appointed long ago? 13 Then I saw that wisdom hath more profit than folly, as light hath more profit than darkness. 14 The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all. 15 Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity. 16 For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that as of old, so the days to come shall all be forgotten. And how dieth the wise man? as the fool. 17 Therefore I hated life; because the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous unto me: for all is vanity and vexation of spirit. 18 Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. 19 And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This is also vanity.

2.9.1.en: The author draws a comparison between wisdom and folly, presenting the following experience:

2.10.0.en: a. "I saw that wisdom hath more profit than folly, as light hath more profit than darkness" [13]. The Preacher does not ignore natural wisdom or the wisdom that comes from human experience, likening wisdom to light and folly to darkness. Wisdom is useful but does not satisfy; but the Lord Christ, who is the heavenly wisdom of God, is both useful and satisfying; He is the light that lighteth every man that cometh into the world, dispelling the darkness of our corruption and offering Himself to us as wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

2.10.1.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that wisdom is useful even for the poor man, because it gives him light so that he does not live in darkness, whereas ignorance destroys the rich man, who in his greed and love of money lives in a darkness that does not let him see things as he ought. One who stands in a dark place does not see what is around him, even if it is a vessel of gold or a precious stone or costly garments... he counts them all as nothing, does not appreciate their value and does not see their beauty; so the greedy man does not perceive the value of the things worthy of our concern.

2.10.2.en: Let us enjoy the Lord Christ, the true "Wisdom," and be enlightened by His Holy Spirit, the giver of love, joy and peace... And let us leave folly, lest we care for dust and do not care for heaven! Folly is a darkness that corrupts our view of God and His Kingdom, and even of ourselves and our brethren, as well as of the world and all that is in it!

2.10.3.en: * How great is the difference between wisdom and folly; they differ as day differs from night.

2.10.4.en: He who chooses virtue is like one who sees all things with perfect clarity, like one who looks upward and walks his paths in the brightness of the light. But he who, on the other hand, has plunged into evil is like a person wandering aimlessly on a moonless night, walking like a blind man, deprived of seeing things, like one who is in darkness. And when I contemplate the end of those patterns of life, I find no profit in the end. And as I accompany the fool, I receive the wages of folly, for what is the use of those thoughts, and what is the benefit of this multitude of words which the fool utters, since they are, so to speak, flowing from an overflow of folly?!

2.10.5.en: Also there is nothing in common between the wise man and the fool, neither as regards the remembrance of man nor God's recompense of them... The wise man never shares the fool's end. Therefore I hated my whole life, that which vanities consumed, and which I spent with a mind burdened with earthly cares.

2.10.6.en: St. Gregory the Wonderworker St. Basil the Great speaks to us about the importance of human wisdom, philosophy and the sciences, without exaggeration or ignoring of divine wisdom:

2.10.7.en: * In my opinion every sensible man thinks that learning is the chief of all that is good and within the reach of our minds. And I do not say that only our own learning is high and noble, because it despises outward elegance to cling to the beauty of thoughts, but also the learning from outside, which many Christians of little esteem reject and consider deceptive and a danger that draws us away from God... Therefore we must keep what can help us to contemplate the truth, avoiding everything that leads to evil, error and destruction.

2.10.8.en: * We must begin by reading worldly thought in order to rise afterward to the holy things and the mysteries of the faith... If there is agreement between this culture and our doctrines, knowing it is of great benefit; and if not, the comparison in the opposite case will confirm our correct beliefs.

2.10.9.en: * It is very important for us not to throw ourselves ignorantly into the sciences, but to know which of them is the most useful... and, for fear that we may cling to them and forget the knowledge of God, immersed in vain researches, he shows the necessity of discernment in education, in such a way that we choose useful learning and avoid everything harmful and ominous.

2.11.0.en: St. Basil the Great b. The Preacher connects wisdom with righteousness, and folly with evil, for he says: "The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness" [14]. The spiritual man is the wise man who fixes his eyes on the Lord Christ as the head of the Church, looking to Him in all his temporal and spiritual affairs, because the eyes point to looking to temporal life (the left eye) and eternal life (the right eye). The wise spiritual man sees that the Lord Christ is the center of his present and eternal life, but the fool walks in darkness, that is, in the circle of sin outside Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.

2.11.1.en: * "The wise man's eyes are in his head"; in which head? Every man, even the dull and the foolish, has his eyes in his bodily head, but the wise man has eyes (these that I just spoke of, which have been enlightened by the Lord's commandments) in his head, that is, in Christ, because "Christ is the head of the man," as the Apostle says.

2.11.2.en: Christ is the One at work in our mind.

2.11.3.en: Origen The wise man's eyes are in his head, that is, in the heavenly Lord Christ; therefore his heart also is lifted to heaven and reaches the summit, and does not remain in the mire of this world and its dust. St. Ambrose says: [The heart is all the more above the summit, because the wise man's eyes are in his head].

2.11.4.en: St. Isaac the Syrian sees that this is realized by enjoying the wisdom stored up in the words of Holy Scripture, for as the wise man is always looking to Christ the Head, that is, to the heavenly Word, his heart is lifted to behold the heavenly things.

2.11.5.en: * When a man's thoughts are wholly immersed in the delight of pursuing the wisdom stored up in the words of Holy Scripture, by his own will, gained through enlightenment from them, he puts the world behind his back and forgets everything in it, and wipes from his soul all memories that embody the world for him. Indeed, he often begins to forget ordinary thoughts that spring from the notions of human nature, and his soul remains in a state of wonder (a divine vision, ecstasy) because of the new thoughts that stir within it, arising from the sea of the mysteries of Holy Scripture.

2.11.6.en: St. Isaac the Syrian c. As for human wisdom, it is unable to lift man to the enjoyment of eternal life, or to renew his corrupt nature; so with all its usefulness it does not differ from folly, for the following reasons:

2.11.7.en: First: temporal wisdom does not carry us to what is above time; therefore, as the fool is subject to death, so the life of the wise man ends in death.

2.11.8.en: "And I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all; then said I in my heart,

2.11.9.en: As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me.

2.11.10.en: And why was I then more wise?

2.11.11.en: Then I said in my heart,

2.11.13.en: And how dieth the wise man? as the fool!" [14-16].

2.11.14.en: Even if temporal wisdom is useful like light, it is powerless; it cannot face death or challenge it! By human wisdom and science man has advanced and satisfied many of his needs, even though his thirst for new aspirations has increased all the more; but what science cannot do is to conquer death. In Christ Jesus alone, the wisdom of God, I am able to face death, singing:

2.11.15.en: "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death...

2.11.16.en: Death is swallowed up in victory.

2.11.17.en: O death, where is thy sting?

2.11.18.en: O grave, where is thy victory...?

2.11.19.en: But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!" (1 Cor 15:26, 54-57).

2.12.0.en: b. Temporal wisdom gives man temporal glory and fame that may reach the ends of the earth, so that man thinks himself immortal on earth, or that his name will not be blotted out from among the sons of men... But the days pass and the wise man is forgotten just like the fool. "For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that as of old, so the days to come shall all be forgotten" [16]. We look to past time as something that has ended, and the coming days will look to our age as an old time that has been forgotten!

2.12.1.en: He who binds himself to the wheel of time, which turns with it up and down, remains in constant change, and then his remembrance ends with time; but he who binds his life to the eternal life of Christ, his life becomes continual ascents, and he enjoys strength upon strength, and grace instead of grace, and the days increase his splendor, and his glory is manifested in the great day of the Lord, and he is never forgotten!

2.13.0.en: c. Perhaps the wise man does not care about his life or his remembrance, reckoning that what he gathers by his experience, skill and wisdom remains for his heirs... but he does not know what they will do with what he acquired by his striving and toil. Therefore he says: "Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity" [18-19].

2.13.1.en: The wise man does not know what his heirs will do with what he acquired, but he who is bound to heavenly wisdom bequeaths to them a blessing that is not lost. What did Zacharias the priest and Elizabeth bequeath to St. John the Baptist? Their constant holy prayers and their righteousness in the Lord... so their life was a support to him while he was in the wilderness, deprived of their visible care!

2.13.2.en: Past generations handed down to us the deposit of the living Tradition, that is, practical faith in the Holy Trinity and the experience of a sincere Gospel life, as an inheritance for us to live under all circumstances, a priceless treasure! And we also must live the same living Gospel Tradition to hand it on as an inheritance to the coming generations, a mystery of blessing for many! The Church's projects or temporal possessions may be lost, but her faith is her living capital, the practical inheritance that the generations receive as their own!

2.14.0.en: Since man does not know what will befall him in the future or what his heirs will do with his labor, he lives his days in grief and sorrows, and in the night his heart takes no rest [23]; but he who is occupied with the pearl of great price, with the Lord Christ Himself, does not fear the future as though it were unknown! The first enters unconsciously into a state of despair and says: "Therefore I hated life... Yea, I hated all my labour" [17-18]; but the second, with joyful hope, says: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."

2.15.0.en: 20 Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour which I took under the sun. 21 For there is a man whose labour is in wisdom, and in knowledge, and in success; yet to a man that hath not laboured therein shall he leave it for his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil. 22 For what hath man of all his labour, and of the diligence of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? 23 For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.

2.15.1.en: The wise man hates life and even hates toil [17-18], for he sees it as worthless... He toils to gather fruits that fall into the grasp of another, perhaps a fool and indifferent, or into the hand of a man who does nothing to deserve to receive that wealth...

2.15.2.en: "Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour which I took under the sun" [20].

2.15.3.en: He who is bound to temporal wisdom suffers from despair and misery, but he who is bound to divine wisdom enjoys joyful heavenly hope.

2.15.4.en: * The good man who receives wisdom from God also enjoys heavenly joy; on the other hand, the wicked man, struck by the diseases that God allows for him, and immersed in the sickness of lust, who toils for more, is soon put to shame by the one whom God has honored... for the wicked man prefers useless gifts and pursues deceit and vanities with his wretched soul.

2.15.5.en: St. Gregory the Wonderworker The wise man is not occupied with what surrounds his self (the concerns of the body), nor with what belongs to him of health, beauty and pleasure, but cares for his very self, for it is better than everything. St. Basil the Great says: [Take heed to yourself (Deut 15:9), for it is the precious treasure and the greatest good, and it deserves your keenest care... So do not care for the body nor for what is connected with the body, such as health and beauty, pleasure and long life. Likewise do not pay great attention to wealth, glory and authority, and all that is connected with earthly life. But care for yourself above everything... adorn it with virtues, cleanse it from sin, and beautify it with the adornment of virtue, which is the most beautiful adornment].

2.16.s.en: 5. Enjoying the pleasures of ordinary life given by God:

2.16.0.en: 24 There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God. 25 For who eateth, and who enjoyeth, more than I? 26 For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit.

2.16.1.en: Lest it be thought that the author pushes us toward despair or distorts the image of the world and the body, which God created for us, he offers us practical advice, which is that we accept the circumstances in which we live and enjoy life as far as possible, looking at everything, even eating and drinking and the ability to work and toil, as a divine gift, since God has given us this life and has planned it as it is.

2.16.2.en: "There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul see (taste) good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God" [24].

2.16.3.en: He does not say let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die, as the Stoics, lovers of pleasures, said, but rather let us eat, drink and work giving thanks to God, who gives us everything, even the possibility of eating, drinking and working.

2.16.4.en: He does not push us toward "escapism," that is, escaping from responsibilities and real troubles by plunging into pleasures and a life of amusement and fantasy, like drug addiction, but urges us to practice real life, giving thanks to God.

2.16.5.en: St. Augustine sees that the Preacher invites us to the fellowship of the table of the Eucharist, which the Lord Christ instituted with His body and blood given for us, as the Mediator of the New Covenant and the Priest after the order of Melchizedek, so that we eat and drink in a spirit of thanksgiving.

2.16.6.en: We can say that the Preacher, in this chapter, while affirming the vanity of temporal pleasures, invites us to go out of the world, not going out in the body but in the heart, so that we may not be entangled in its cares nor absorbed by its pleasures, but depart to the age to come with thanksgiving and joy.

2.16.7.en: * No one draws near to God except the one who has separated himself from the world; but by separation I do not mean departing from the body, but departing from (entanglement) in the affairs of the world.

2.16.8.en: * Blessed is he who has not lost his way of life in this vain world and on this great sea!

2.16.9.en: Blessed is the man whose ship has not been wrecked, and who has reached the harbor with joy.

2.16.10.en: St. Isaac the Syrian His call to us to enjoy the pleasures of ordinary life given by God confirms the Preacher's view of creation, that it is good, and that its vanity depends on our wrong view of it or our misuse of it.

2.16.11.en: * Idle wealth is of no use, but it becomes fertile and fruitful if its use is regulated.

2.16.12.en: * Creatures are not evil by their nature; had they been evil, God would not have created them, since every creature of God is good, as the Apostle Paul said (1 Tim 4:4), and His commandment does not order us to reject good things and flee from them, but to manage them well; and no one is condemned for owning wealth, but for boasting of it or for misusing it.

2.16.13.en: St. Basil the Great The Preacher's words here are an invitation to a life of joyful work, for he says:

2.16.14.en: "There is nothing better for a man than that... he should make his soul see good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God" [24].

2.16.15.en: If we thank God for the food and drink He has given us, we thank Him also because He has granted us to toil, working with pleasure and joy, working not only in the life of worship but in our ordinary daily life. St. Basil the Great has delightful discourses on "work," even for monks.

2.16.16.en: * Since our Lord Jesus Christ said, "The worker is worthy of his wages" (Mt 10:10), and not just anyone at all and anyhow, and the Apostle commanded us to toil and to work with our hands what is good so that we may have something to share with the needy (Eph 4:28), it is therefore clear that we must work diligently, for it is not permitted to us to make worship a pretext for idleness and for fleeing from toil...

2.16.17.en: And since some disdain work on the pretext of prayers and singing psalms, such people should know that everything has its own time, as the Preacher said: "To every thing there is a season" (Eccl 3:1).

2.16.18.en: * The prohibition of excessive care for the needs of our body does not negate care and work altogether. For it remains for us "to work for ourselves, not for the food which perisheth, but for the food which endureth unto everlasting life" (Jn 6:27). And the Lord will say to us on the Day of Judgment: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink" (Mt 25:35, etc.). And on the contrary, He will punish those who did not work and did not toil to help the weak and to serve their neighbor (Acts 20:4), and will send them to torment (Mt 25:21). Work, then, on this understanding, orders social relations in the best way and gives them an atmosphere of mutual support and harmony.

2.16.19.en: * Everyone must attend to his own particular work and care for it willingly and fulfil it blamelessly with zeal, diligence, care and watchfulness, lest he deserve the curse, for it is said: "Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord slackly" (Jer 48:10)...

2.16.20.en: It is better for us to undertake one work with discipline and precision than to do many works without finish. For distraction among many occupations and moving from one thing to another so that none of them is accomplished is a sign of a levity rooted in nature or a cause of the generation of that levity.
